title: “I’d Like a Report on What the U.S. Does Against Drugs,” Sheinbaum Says
author: Romina Gándara
content:
_This article by[Romina
Gándara](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/sugeyry_gandara/) originally
appeared in the [September 17, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4871947/la-presidenta-me-gustaria-un-
reporte-de-eu-sobre-lo-que-eu-hace-contra-las-drogas/), one of Mexico’s
leading independent digital news outlets._

**Mexico City, September 17 (SinEmbargo).—** President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo
(CSP) questioned on Thursday that the United States (U.S.) government is
evaluating Mexico’s efforts against drug trafficking, and **proposed that the
neighboring country also present a report on the actions it takes to combat
the consumption and distribution of substances.**

Asked about the U.S. anti-drug report, the Mexican president warned that the
fight against drug trafficking does not fall only on producing or transit
countries, but also on curbing consumption, distribution, and money laundering
within U.S. territory.

“I would like to hear or see a report on what the United States government
does inside the United States. We’ve said here many times… President [Donald]
Trump acknowledged it at some point and it is acknowledged in a document from
the so-called ‘anti-drug strategy,’ that letter: What is being done about
consumption?” she said at her morning press conference.

President Sheinbaum Pardo noted that Mexico has insisted that drug consumption
must also be addressed as a public health problem, particularly among young
people.

At the same time, she affirmed that the Mexican government maintains its fight
against those who produce and traffic substances into the U.S.: “No one agrees
that drugs should be produced here to take them to the United States, and we
have to work so that this does not happen.”

However, she called for reviewing what measures President Donald Trump’s
administration applies against consumption and distribution networks. She even
**questioned the lack of information about actions against money laundering
related to drug trafficking.**

> The firepower that organized crime has in our country could not be explained
> without the passage of weapons from the United States into Mexico illegally.
>
> Claudia Sheinbaum

The Mexican president cited as an example the opioid crisis the U.S. faces and
recalled that part of the problem began with prescription painkillers
authorized despite prior warnings about their high addictive potential.

“The firepower that organized crime has in our country could not be explained
without the passage of weapons from the United States into Mexico illegally,”
she maintained.

On the country’s results, she stressed that Mexico acts at home: there are
arrests, drug seizures, and investigations against complicit officials,
regardless of the party they belong to.

She also mentioned a case involving DEA agents who were accused of allowing
the trafficking and sale of fentanyl in New Mexico. “**We do not need to be
judged from the outside.** We know what Mexico’s problems are and we act every
day and we report it,” she emphasized.

The head of the Executive branch acknowledged that her government is
permanently subject to public scrutiny and that accountability does not occur
solely through annual reports.

“We render accounts every day and we are subject to public scrutiny every day
and every day we deliver results,” she said.

For that reason, she reiterated that it would also be necessary to know the
results of the actions undertaken by the United States within its own
territory.

**“But what is happening over there? So I would like to see a report from the
government itself on the results there and what is being done,” she
concluded.**
